title: Design a URL Shortener
description: Design a service like bit.ly that takes a long URL and returns a short alias. The system should redirect users to the original URL when the alias is accessed. Consider read-heavy traffic, collision handling, and analytics.

hints.no_cache: A URL shortener is extremely read-heavy. Without a cache layer, every redirect hits the DB.
hints.no_load_balancer: At scale, a single redirect server is a bottleneck and single point of failure. A load balancer is needed to distribute traffic across multiple instances.

componentRoles.CLIENT: The user or browser making a request to shorten a URL or follow a short link.
componentRoles.LOAD_BALANCER: Distributes redirect and write traffic across multiple API Gateway / service instances to prevent any single node from becoming a bottleneck.
componentRoles.API_GATEWAY: Entry point for all API traffic. Handles short-link resolution requests and routes them to the appropriate service.
componentRoles.SERVICE: Core business logic — generates short codes (hashing / Base62 encoding), checks for collisions, and performs redirects.
componentRoles.CACHE: Stores the most frequently accessed short-code → long-URL mappings so redirects can be served without hitting the database on every request.
componentRoles.DATABASE: Persistent store for all short-code → long-URL mappings, user data, and analytics.

title: Design a Rate Limiter
description: Design a rate limiter that restricts the number of requests a client can make to an API within a time window. It should work in a distributed environment where multiple API servers are running.

hints.no_cache: Rate limiting counters (token bucket state, sliding window counts) must live in a fast in-memory store like Redis — not a relational DB.
hints.no_gateway_cache_link: The API Gateway is where rate limiting logic runs. It must be directly connected to the Cache (Redis) to read and increment request counters on every inbound request.
hints.no_load_balancer: A distributed rate limiter runs across multiple API Gateway instances — a load balancer is required to spread incoming traffic across them.
hints.rate_limit_cache_has_outgoing: The rate-limit cache (Redis) is a pure counter store — it should have no outgoing connections. Only the API Gateway reads and writes to it.

componentRoles.CLIENT: The caller making API requests — could be a user, mobile app, or another service. Each client has a rate limit enforced against it.
componentRoles.LOAD_BALANCER: Spreads traffic across multiple API Gateway instances. For rate limiting to be consistent, all instances must share the same Redis counter store.
componentRoles.API_GATEWAY: This is where rate limiting happens. On every inbound request it reads the client's counter from Redis, increments it, and either forwards the request or rejects it with HTTP 429.
componentRoles.CACHE: Acts as the distributed counter store (Redis). Holds token bucket state or sliding window counts per client. Must be shared across all gateway instances so limits are enforced globally.
componentRoles.SERVICE: The downstream backend that only receives requests that have passed the rate limit check at the gateway.
componentRoles.DATABASE: Persistent store for rate limit configuration (rules, quotas per client/plan) and audit logs.

title: Design Twitter's News Feed
description: Design the news feed feature of Twitter where users see a ranked timeline of tweets from people they follow. Consider fan-out strategies, ranking, and the difference between celebrity and regular user follower counts.

hints.no_async_processing: Pushing tweets to all follower feeds synchronously blocks the write path. A queue is essential for fan-out.
hints.no_cache: Feed reads massively outnumber writes. Without a cache layer, the DB becomes the bottleneck.
hints.no_load_balancer: A news feed serves millions of concurrent reads. Without a load balancer, a single service instance becomes the bottleneck.
hints.single_database: Tweets, user graphs, and precomputed timelines have very different access patterns. A single DB cannot efficiently handle all of them at Twitter's scale.

componentRoles.CLIENT: The Twitter user's app or browser, requesting their home timeline or posting a new tweet.
componentRoles.LOAD_BALANCER: Distributes read (timeline fetch) and write (tweet post) traffic across multiple service instances.
componentRoles.API_GATEWAY: Routes requests to the correct downstream service — timeline reads, tweet writes, or user graph lookups.
componentRoles.SERVICE: Multiple services: fan-out service that pushes new tweets into follower timelines (fan-out-on-write for regular users, fan-out-on-read for celebrities), and the read service that assembles and ranks the feed.
componentRoles.CACHE: Stores precomputed timelines per user. The hot path for feed reads — avoids rebuilding the timeline from the DB on every request.
componentRoles.DATABASE: Multiple stores: one for tweets/content, one for the social graph (follows), and one for precomputed timeline lists.
componentRoles.QUEUE: Decouples tweet ingestion from fan-out. When a user tweets, the event is enqueued and fan-out workers asynchronously push it to follower caches.

title: Design Uber
description: Design Uber's core ride-matching system. Users request rides, nearby drivers are matched, and location is tracked in real time. Consider location indexing, matching latency, and handling high-frequency location updates.

hints.no_cache: Driver locations update every few seconds. A geospatial cache (e.g. Redis Geo) is required to query nearby drivers with low latency.
hints.single_database: Location updates from millions of drivers require a purpose-built geospatial store (e.g., Redis Geo, PostGIS) separate from the ride/user OLTP database.
hints.no_async_processing: Location updates arrive at very high frequency. Processing them synchronously on the write path creates unacceptable latency — use a queue to decouple ingestion from processing.
hints.no_load_balancer: High-frequency location updates from millions of concurrent drivers require horizontal scaling behind a load balancer.

componentRoles.CLIENT: The rider app (requesting a ride) or driver app (streaming location updates every few seconds).
componentRoles.LOAD_BALANCER: Distributes the high volume of location update requests and ride-matching requests across service instances.
componentRoles.API_GATEWAY: Entry point for all client traffic. Routes location pings, ride requests, and status updates to the appropriate backend service.
componentRoles.SERVICE: Multiple services: location ingestion (writes driver position), matching service (finds nearest available driver using geospatial index), and trip management service.
componentRoles.CACHE: Geospatial store (Redis Geo) holding live driver positions. Enables sub-millisecond nearest-driver queries without hitting the main database.
componentRoles.DATABASE: Persistent store for trips, user profiles, ride history, and billing. Separate from the geospatial cache.
componentRoles.QUEUE: Buffers the firehose of location updates from millions of drivers so the ingestion service isn't overwhelmed on the synchronous path.

title: Design YouTube
description: Design YouTube's video upload, storage, and streaming infrastructure. Users upload videos which are processed into multiple resolutions and streamed globally. Consider large file handling, transcoding pipelines, and CDN delivery.

hints.no_cdn: Streaming video to a global audience without a CDN means all traffic hits your origin servers — infeasible at scale.
hints.no_object_storage: Videos cannot live in a relational DB. Object storage (S3-equivalent) is required for large binary files.
hints.no_async_processing: Video transcoding is CPU-intensive and long-running. It must be handled asynchronously via a queue and worker pool.
hints.no_load_balancer: Video upload and metadata API traffic must be distributed across multiple service instances. A load balancer is essential.
hints.no_cache: Video metadata (titles, thumbnails, view counts) is read far more than it is written. Without a cache layer, every page load hammers the database.

componentRoles.CLIENT: The viewer (streaming video) or creator (uploading video). Viewers hit the CDN for video data; creators hit the API for uploads.
componentRoles.LOAD_BALANCER: Distributes upload and metadata API requests across multiple service instances.
componentRoles.API_GATEWAY: Handles all API traffic — upload initiation, metadata fetches, search, and recommendations.
componentRoles.SERVICE: Multiple services: upload service (receives chunks, stores to object storage), transcoding worker (consumes from queue, produces multiple resolutions), and metadata/recommendation service.
componentRoles.CACHE: Stores video metadata (title, thumbnail URL, view count, description) to serve page loads without hitting the database on every request.
componentRoles.DATABASE: Persistent store for video metadata, user data, comments, subscriptions, and view counts.
componentRoles.QUEUE: Decouples upload completion from transcoding. When a raw video is uploaded, a job is enqueued and transcoding workers pick it up asynchronously.
componentRoles.OBJECT_STORAGE: Stores raw uploaded video files and all transcoded renditions (360p, 720p, 1080p, etc.). The source of truth for all video bytes.
componentRoles.CDN: Caches and serves video segments to viewers from edge nodes close to them. Eliminates origin load for the vast majority of playback traffic.

title: Design WhatsApp
description: Design WhatsApp's messaging system supporting one-to-one and group messaging with delivery and read receipts. Consider message ordering, offline delivery, end-to-end encryption architecture, and handling billions of messages per day.

hints.no_async_processing: Message delivery to offline users requires a persistent queue — you cannot rely on a live connection being available.
hints.single_database: At billions of messages per day, a single DB is not viable. Messages and user/session data should be in separate stores, sharded by user or conversation ID.
hints.no_cache: User presence, session state, and recent message history are read constantly. A cache layer (e.g. Redis) is essential to avoid DB overload.
hints.no_load_balancer: Billions of daily messages across hundreds of millions of users require horizontally scaled service nodes behind a load balancer.

componentRoles.CLIENT: A user's mobile app, maintaining a persistent WebSocket connection to the messaging service for real-time delivery.
componentRoles.LOAD_BALANCER: Routes WebSocket connections and API requests across messaging service nodes. Connection affinity (sticky sessions) may be needed for WebSocket.
componentRoles.API_GATEWAY: Handles REST API calls (registration, key exchange, profile updates) and proxies WebSocket upgrade requests to the messaging service.
componentRoles.SERVICE: Multiple services: connection manager (holds open WebSocket connections), message router (delivers to online users or enqueues for offline), and notification service (push notifications).
componentRoles.CACHE: Stores user presence (online/offline), active WebSocket session mappings, and recent message history for fast delivery status lookups.
componentRoles.DATABASE: Sharded message store (by conversation ID) and separate user/profile store. Messages are persisted for delivery guarantees and history.
componentRoles.QUEUE: Buffers messages for offline users. When the recipient comes online, the queue is drained and messages are delivered in order.
